newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Bosnian leaders agree central bank law - governor.
newsitem.headline: Bosnian leaders agree central bank law - governor.

text.p: Bosnia's Moslem, Croat and Serb leaders have agreed on a draft law to form a single central bank, clearing the way for a peacetime monetary system, bank governor Serge Robert said on Thursday.
A U.S. delegation led by special envoy Robert Gelbard announced the deal after mediating negotiations with members of the collective presidency late on Wednesday night.
Foreign experts said the draft law, which still has to be adopted by the joint inter-ethnic parliament, granted some concessions sought by Serb leaders.

The law would allow the country's Serb republic, which together with a Moslem-Croat federation comprises Bosnia, to continue to use currency from neighbouring Yugoslavia for some official transactions.

For payments to the central government or to the federation, the law would require Serb authorities to use the new Bosnian currency, known as the "convertible marka", said Robert, the French governor of the central bank.
But for taxes and private transactions inside the Serb republic, the draft law would permit the use of the Yugoslav dinar over an interim period, Robert told Reuters.
"It's just because this part of Bosnia-Herzegovina is so much integrated into the economy of Belgrade (Yugoslavia)," Robert said.
He said there was no deadline set for the transition period but he said the IMF would conduct quarterly surveys to monitor the functioning of the monetary system.
"It will depend on IMF recommendations to the presidency," he said.
The governor said he welcomed the agreement as an important step towards establishing the bank, which will operate as a currency board with a fixed exchange rate and full reserve backing.
A myriad of technical details had yet to be worked out, he said. "Recognition of the symbolic signficance of the agreement should not ignore the operational challenges ahead," he said.

Under the draft law, the bank's headquarters would be located primarily in Sarajevo and some offices would be opened in Serb-controlled territory in the suburb of Lukavica or in Pale, 16 km (10 miles) outside the city.
The bank would have two branch offices, one in the southwest town of Mostar in the federation and the other in the Serb entity, he said.

The law includes provisions for an interim currency design until a permanent currency is introduced in Bosnia. Serb and Moslem-Croat territories will each have their own design for the same currency but neither has approved a design yet.

The interim currency should be introduced soon, said David Lipton of the U.S. Treasury Department, who helped mediate the negotiations. "It's a matter of months, probably little more than two months," Lipton said.

Forming a central bank is an element crucial to clinching a deal with the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and for securing $1.4 billion expected to be raised at a donors' conference for post-war reconstruction.

Apart from the central bank law, the IMF has also called for an agreement on the new currency and a timetable for its introduction, budget laws, uniform tariffs and a law on servicing of Bosnia's external debt.
